utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. IT-95-14/2-T, The Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Everybody seems to be standing up. Mr. Jennings, would you like to take a seat for the moment, please, while we deal with these matters. Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour. The Prosecution was kind enough to send us over last night the final version of the outline of the testimony of this witness, and I would just like to inform the Court that we do not object to the Prosecution leading a large part of the evidence, with the exception of certain specified paragraphs, which I would like to relate to the Court right now, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Sayers. Did you say, if I heard well, 26 to 40, from 26 to 40?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there any objection to the witness having a copy of the summary?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I don't think so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please. THE COURT: If you would like to take the declaration, Major.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a small number of exhibit --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There is a small number of exhibits to be produced by this witness. I've had them put together in chronological order. May they now be distributed to the Chamber. Examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Chamber may find it helpful, without otherwise disturbing the selection of exhibits, to look a little over halfway through for a black-and-white, a three-sized map, and possibly to take it out, although it may in due course return to its position in the sequence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Number?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's 2781,1. The reason I suggest to take it out is this: As you'll hear from the witness, this is part of a map that was provided to him by Mr. Kordic, and he keeps the original of it. It happens to be a very good map in terms of the detail it provides. I've asked the witness, with the help of the usher, to leave the coloured original on the ELMO so that it can, I think, now be seen. It may prove a useful, regular point of reference for us. It's worth noting immediately, that although the map is, I think, thought by the witness to be accurate, it bears different grid lines and different grid line numberings from the other map, with which we are more familiar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Philip Francis Andrew Jennings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are presently a Major?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A career officer?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the Cheshire Regiment?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Presently studying within your career for a master of philosophy degree at Newcastle University?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Being deployed in the former Yugoslavia in the early part of 1993, taking command of a company there on the 13th of January?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The operations area that was your responsibility, can you show it on the ELMO? We'll just check that our video is working. It wasn't working earlier. Your Honour, I don't know if the Court has a picture. We don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What are they doing? It's working.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: The map which you can see shows part of the area, of my area of operational responsibility. You can just bring it out more and do a slight refold. Excuse me a moment, please. If I go from west to east, the area of operational responsibility covered past Vitez, which is shown here, up to the town of Travnik, past it to Turbe, which was actually the front line between the opposing forces at the time and down to a place called Novi Travnik. Through Vitez itself, down towards a bridge which I called the Kaonik Bridge, and then going south on this road through Busovaca, and down on that road to where it met Sarajevo just south of Kiseljak. A mountain road going over the top to the town of Zenica and the road which went from the Kaonik Bridge through a place called Luke, which then -- it's just off the map here -- looped around and was the main approach route to Zenica. That, and just off the road, were the main areas of my responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the UNPROFOR mission to support UNHCR in the delivery of humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Yes, the UNPROFOR mission was to conduct operation in support of UNHCR in order to -- that being the key; those are the key words: deliver humanitarian aid. And it was up to us to interpret at that mission to ensure that that aid was delivered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Incidentally, Major Jennings, the reason I pause is to ensure that interpreters catch up. Were there two main approaches, one from Mostar via Busovaca and the second via Prozor and Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: That is correct. These were the two main supply routes from the coast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your commanding officer was Colonel Stewart. With his approval, although you were commanding a company, did you carry out certain liaison officer functions, concentrating those functions on Busovaca, Kacuni -- and if you want to point them out as I speak them, do -- Busovaca, Kacuni --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Just a moment. I'll move the map again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Merdani?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: So Busovaca, Kacuni [Indicating].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Merdani, and Katici, the purpose of these liaison functions being to learn about local commanders on both sides, HVO and ABiH, and pursuant to what the army calls an implied task to negotiate with them?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Although you were performing some of these liaison functions, the official liaison officers at the time were Martyn Forgrave, for Novi Travnik and Travnik, and Matthew Dundas-Whatley for Zenica?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet the BiH commanders, Kulenovic for Travnik, Refik Lendo for Novi Travnik; the HVO commander, Colonel Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the 20th of January, at a meeting attended by Forgrave, did Kulenovic inform you that the situation in Travnik was tense, such that a small incident could spark off a Muslim/Croat clash?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you or all of you assessed this as being probably a genuine depiction of the position?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: That is what we felt at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The HVO had a checkpoint on the main Travnik/Novi Travnik junction -- which you can just identify for us, if it's shown on that map --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: I think it's just --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's just off, is it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: It's just off the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We know it, in any event; we're familiar with that -- which was reinforced with HVO soldiers and a twin 30-millimetre gun mounted on a flat-bed truck?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 21st of January, in Vitez, at a conference, was it stated that the ABiH had set up a new checkpoint in Busovaca, and this was interpreted as an increase in tension; and that day or night, were there eight explosions recorded within the Muslim enclave, the HVO having set up checkpoints at either end of the town?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: That is correct. All of this was reported at the daily 5.00 conference by the milinfo section, which I remember at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You travelled to Tuzla on the 22nd, returning on the 24th of January, to discover that the situation in Kacuni was serious, two Croats having been killed when a gun was fired at their vehicle which had slipped into a convoy?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard of this, I think, from the adjutant who had gone to Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: I heard it on the high-frequency net on my Land Rover, and I listened to the reports, as did everyone else on the net, as they were coming in, as the situation unfolded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went to collect the bodies and assessed that in the two days you'd been away, tension in the area had risen from tolerable to high?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you informed of a lorry placed across the road at Kacuni by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: I was informed of this on the evening of the 24th of January at the time that I was tasked to go out and collect or to supervise the collection of the two Croat bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you got to the junction -- which you might point out for us --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: The junction in question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. You headed on the road south to Busovaca to get to Kacuni, and I think at a T-junction, you came across a firefight?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: That's correct. This was very early on the morning of the 25th. I was informed that the lorry, which contained logs, had been placed across the road -- in the headquarters in Vitez I was informed of this, but we decided not to actually go out until first light on the morning of the 25th, and the incident in question took place here [indicates], at this T-junction, where there was a bridge. The name place is Kaonik. And the firefight was intense, an intense amount of single machine-gun fire, and quite a large number of soldiers on either side of the river.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You returned to Vitez to discuss the situation with Colonel Stewart; both of you headed for Kacuni the same day, to discover buildings on the main northern approach to Busovaca on fire, the evidence suggesting a hurried departure by residents: For example, laundry was smouldering, left outside smouldering, along with houses that were burning; things like that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Busovaca had been subject to explosion and fire, recent explosion and fire, and your assessment was that explosions had occurred there prior to the outbreak of fighting on the 24th of January; you discovered new roadblocks, manned by the HVO, which it was not possible to bypass, one at the north and one at the south of the town?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As recently as the 11th to the 16th of January, you having travelled the same area and found it safe to travel in a single armoured Land Rover?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: That's correct. A point worth making is that we felt safe travelling in a Land Rover on its own, and we had clear guidelines as to what type of vehicle could go out on the road, whether it was a Warrior or a Land Rover, whether it could go on its own or in pairs, dependent on the assessed situation and how dangerous it was deemed to be. And at that time, between the 11th and the 16th, there was free movement of single vehicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 25th of January, did you, in convoy with Colonel Stewart, reach Kacuni --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- stopping some 40 metres short of the bridge to discover that a lorry with flattened tires blocked the road to anyone approaching from the north? If you would just like to indicate again on the map, and I'll read on.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see HVO soldiers who had moved into buildings no more than two to three hundred metres away in the northern outskirts of Kacuni, and some time later, did then-Brigadier Cordy-Simpson arrive from the south, he, with Colonel Stewart, negotiating the removal of the lorry, which was eventually removed; but during this time, did you see HVO soldiers move into position with a Wombat-type weapon which the HVO then fired directly at civilian houses in Kacuni with very destructive effect, the houses being targeted effectively for summary destruction, there being no justification for the military action taken, apart from a single and apparently accidental or negligent discharge of one rifle by one ABiH soldier in the area?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the opinion that I made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is a Wombat type of weapon?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the expression is actually the description of a weapon that was in the British armed services when I first joined, but I was subsequently shown pictures of types of weapons, and I identified it as a ZIS-2. This is a wheeled, long-barrelled anti-tank weapon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the Court would turn now to its bundle of exhibits, and if you'd just look at them again with us. The first one is a map which has been marked, which we can probably put on one side. It was marked by you on an earlier occasion, I think?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And identifies various places. I'll endeavour to remember to deal with it right at the end of your evidence, see if there is anything we've missed. Does the second sheet, Exhibit 862,2, show the ZIS-2 Wombat type weapon to which you've referred?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the weapon which I identified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 12. Did you intend to accompany Colonel Stewart to Kiseljak, but for mechanical reasons had to stay for some eight hours before your Warrior vehicle could move, and during that time was there intense fighting consistent and increasing, or increased between the HVO and the ABiH until nightfall?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the following day, the 26th of January, did you return to Kacuni to see the commander, on instructions to clear the bridge, knowing in advance that it would not have been cleared because the dispute had not been resolved? Was there a large explosion next to your vehicle, which skidded across or off the road? Did you find the lorry still blocking the road, and were the BiH refusing to move it, saying that they anticipated an attack? Colonel Stewart arrived with the 3rd Corps Deputy Commander Merdan, an agreement was reached that BritBat would man the bridges as an U.N. checkpoint, allowing only U.N. and ICRC vehicles to pass?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stayed at the bridge with the ABiH Commander Sabit, who told you that they were expecting an HVO offensive, three rounds of heavy artillery exploded some 10 metres from you, only half an hour after Colonel Stewart's departure, and one Warrior, indeed, was hit from high ground to the north of Kacuni by machine-gun fire?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to judge, from your experience, the gauge of artillery?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Using my experience in training, I was able to judge it was on or around at least 120 millimetre, because I had observed at close quarters such type of fire during training.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any obvious military targets in this area? Was there any need for the HVO to use military force in this area?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Whilst there were some BiH in the houses, and this is the north end of Kacuni next to the bridge where we had established a checkpoint, there were no obvious defensive and certainly no obvious offensive positions. And in my opinion, I felt that the use of such heavy indirect fire, weapons, was not justified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you judge to be the intended target?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: As is related in my testimony, when I actually first arrived on the morning of the 26th, there was an explosion next to my Warrior as I approached the bridge, which caused me to skid off the road. Following the three rounds of artillery fire, again related in my testimony, the indirect fire actually continued for an hour or so, of an intensive nature, falling on or around my positions. I had four Warriors with me. I drew the conclusion that I was probably the target of this artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you think that there were no Muslims residing in the houses which you'd seen being destroyed, identifying them nevertheless as Muslim because of their four-sided as opposed to ridged-roof structure? The damage to these houses effected by long-range artillery and Wombat-type small-calibre anti-tank weapon that we've seen being fired at a range of a few hundred metres had some Croat houses, apparently, being caught and incidentally damaged, none actually showing signs of being targeted?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: I saw no Croat-styled houses being targeted by this ZIS-2 weapon. I observed firing on the 25th of January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You identify in your summary that it was at Proscica, north of Busovaca-Kacuni road, that you had actually seen the gun being fired?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: That is correct. It was positioned about 50 to 60 metres off the main road, but clearly visible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The ABiH, to your knowledge, had no artillery pieces in the area, and prior to the shelling, from the 25th to the 29th of January, had you seen one artillery piece in Busovaca belonging to the HVO, a long-barrelled weapon folded and ready to be moved?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you deem the use of artillery totally -- on Kacuni to be totally unwarranted, and with your knowledge of the way armies operate, did you assess that instructions for such a shelling could not have come from a junior, but must have come from a senior commander, not least because the HVO artillery had limited artillery fire power, and a decision to deploy limited resources could not have been taken at a junior level?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: That was my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what you observed was at a time when it was dangerous to get out of the vehicle, but despite that, were you able to make an assessment, based on experience, of where the artillery was being fired from?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: I was able to make a rough assessment, and I must stress, a rough assessment. This was based on specific training that I had received, which I could go into detail if you wished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the time being, can we have the conclusion, in case the matter is not challenged, and then we needn't trouble. What was your conclusion as to this source of the artillery?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: I believed that it was coming from the north, northwest from the area of Busovaca itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, just tell us this: As part of your method of assessing the source of the artillery, did you look at the craters left by artillery shells?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: When I felt it was safe to do so, I got out of my vehicle and inspected the craters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Lieutenant Fooks an officer reporting to you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Lieutenant Fooks was directly under my command in C company. He was my troop commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have any particular skills?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He commanded a light reconnaissance troop, one of whose roles is to go out and seek out information. Part of this training is to be able to make a rough assessment of the likely direction of incoming artillery or mortar fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he report to you on his conclusions about the source of this incoming artillery fire?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: That is correct. When I returned to Vitez, as I did as regularly as I could during this three- to four-day period starting from the 25th of January, he had been out on the ground in the rough area carrying out some information duties and had observed this artillery fire and reported to me his conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which were?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: He believed that he was able to hear the sounds of either artillery or mortar fire actually going off and took a compass bearing towards it. He was able to observe from where he was the artillery or mortar fire landing. He also timed the time of flight, and from this was able to make out a rough assessment of where he felt the fire had come from and gave me a grid square, one square kilometre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which was where?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Just to the northwest of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it convenient to show that on this map?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: I can show the rough area on this map, but I believe that the area is actually on the map that you referred to, which was the first exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's take the first exhibit, lay that on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: It relates to these four lines of writing here where I've put in a grid square. And there is an arrow, and going to the right of that, pointing to the grid square, which is an area to the northwest of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The distance from Busovaca to Kacuni being about how far?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: In that area, if that was the area, about five-and-a-half kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whoever was in Busovaca at the time, in your experience, would they have been aware of this use of artillery?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I am not sure that we are going to be helped by evidence of that sort. Anybody is going to be aware that artillery is firing if they are near it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. So be it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This artillery firing went on for how long?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Sporadically, it went on for two to three days, commencing the 25th of January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Paragraph 26, please. On the 26th of January were you patrolling in Donji Polje? Please mark it on whichever map you find convenient. If you find it convenient, mark it on this one.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: It's not marked on this map, but the rough area --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It may be convenient to go to the larger scale map.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: It is okay with this one that I am showing here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can see it, I think, on our own versions because it's been highlighted for us. Thank you. Was that a predominantly Muslim village where you saw two or three HVO soldiers identified by chequerboard red and white patches in camouflage uniform walking out of a Muslim house which, some five minutes later, you saw to be on fire, the location of the house being between Donji Polje and Kacuni? And in that area were some 40 houses over approximately 800 metres, houses that had been systemically burned between the 26th and the 29th of January, there being no ABiH in that region, was your conclusion that the burning must have been by HVO?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: That is correct. The incident is something I personally observed. That is related in my testimony. I had been briefed on the architecture of houses and told that a four-sided roof was a Muslim style. That is where I drew my conclusion. And that it was in the course of patrolling along that specific stretch of road that I saw the steady destruction of these houses. I may not have actually observed every single one being set fire to in the same way, but I did see the end results as I returned every so often each day over several days. And I can say categorically that there were no BiH in that area, none whatsoever. None whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without looking at your summary, please, just help us now in relation to the 27th of January. Did you on that day return to the bridge?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: I did, as I did every day during that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see of the BiH, if anything?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Well, during that period there were very few, I would say probably no more than about 20 to 30, in individual houses. They were a variety of ages. They were only lightly armed. In fact, I only saw one small anti-tank weapon during that period. This is what I would describe as a light anti-tank weapon which is placed on the shoulder. I remember it clearly because it was pointed at me, on the first day I went up to the log lorry itself. But other weapons ranged from Kalashnikovs to shotguns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the BiH command at that time, or in that locality?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: I discovered that the actual headquarters, the name of which I later learnt to be 333 Brigade, was to the south-southwest of where the roadblock had been established and where we had placed a Warrior as a U.N. checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Efforts to meet the officer in command led to your meeting whom?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: I was introduced to a person who was described as a deputy commander. I know that probably his first name was Edin, without referring to my notes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. It may be the name is not challenged; if not, I'll lead it: Veganovic?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And via him, to whom?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: To the commander himself, whose name, without recollection, I can't recall at the moment, but was clearly the commander of 333 Brigade BiH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, if there is no challenge, I'll put the name to you: Anto Sliskovic?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Anto Sliskovic was not -- was -- may I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Unless there is any objection -- is there any objection to these names?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Absolutely none, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Let's --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was the assistant commander; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And you met also Marko Prskalo?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Of the HVO, described to me as a staff officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you actually met these, I think, or you met Sliskovic the following day at DutchBat headquarters in Busovaca; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: It took some time to establish who was who during this period, and I did this mainly with the help of the Dutch transport battalion, which were based just south of Busovaca, my intention being to establish who was in charge locally on each side, to try and bring them together to resolve the dispute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at a meeting with Sliskovic, were things said which you interpreted as some form of promise or threat?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Certainly not a promise, but the atmosphere in the room where I brought together representatives of both sides -- I would describe the BiH representative as a -- definitely a junior deputy commander. The atmosphere from Sliskovic was definitely threatening. I had an interpreter, a very good interpreter, next to me who conveyed exactly what was being said, and the mood, which I could see myself, and the remarks were certainly not helping the situation, which was to establish a sensible discussion between the two sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was something said about civilians detained at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: One of the things which had been said by both sides was the business of people -- civilians being detained. At that meeting, Sliskovic did admit that some Muslims were being held in a camp near Kaonik, and I was able to establish through my milinfo section that there were about 300 of these.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were these people civilians, or military?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: They were civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anything said at this meeting by Sliskovic about the Kacuni shelling which you had seen?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Yes, I clearly remember, it was the only occasion I really brought the subject up about the shelling, which certainly made a powerful impact on me. I inquired why the area had been shelled, and Sliskovic stated that that area where we were had been shelled by the BiH. And I made the comment at the time that I thought it was a ridiculous thing to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By this stage, had you met Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: If we're relating to meetings which took place on and around 28, 29, 30 January, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just yes or no: Was anything said at these meetings in relation to Kordic?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the penultimate sentence of paragraph 21 is slightly out of order, and I'll return to it later. In due course, I think you were to form a view about the relationship between Sliskovic and Kordic, but at this stage, it was too early to form such a view?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Yes. My views were on the basis of what I observed over following weeks, going through February.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next exhibit, please, and the 30th of January. Tell us about this document --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: I have to remove this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- swiftly.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: This was a document that was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just going -- before you speak --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not at all. I'm just going to inform the Court, most of this document, but not quite all of it, has been produced as Defence Exhibit 54/1. Yes, Major.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: This was a document in English, and also in translation, with signatures, which related to a meeting that was held at the school at Bila, the headquarters of U.N. BritBat, chaired by Lieutenant-Colonel Bob Stewart, my commanding officer, on the 30th of January. The significant thing about it is that it details the terms and conditions that were agreed, and that a ceasefire should take place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As to the Kacuni checkpoint, by whom was that to be manned?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: This actually had been agreed on the 25th of January, so therefore it had already been in place. This was the sixth day it had been in place. It was something that was agreed on the ground by Merdan, that the log lorry would be removed if we actually placed a Warrior on that bridge to control the flow of U.N. traffic only, or associated ICRC.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second sheet of this exhibit has the signatures of various people, self-explanatory. The third sheet, which is new to the Chamber, has the printed list of those present -- not printed, the written list of those present at the peace negotiations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 28th of January, did you learn of a DutchBat report concerning Muslim prisoners? Again, don't read from the summary, if you would be so good; just tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just an objection to that, in the absence of laying a proper foundation that this is just first-hand rather than several times removed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the witness read the report, he can tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Sorry, can I be clear to exactly what you're relating to, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. There were some Muslim prisoners referred to in a DutchBat report, and you yourself may have seen some Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before we move on, did you yourself read the report from DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: The report was a verbal report. It was delivered to me in the car park of the Dutch battalion transport headquarters, where I happened to be at the time, and therefore my presence there was coincidental. I was happening to, as it were, be doing my rounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: And I was given a report of a number, 10 to 15 Muslims who were being forced to dig graves in a local graveyard with HVO soldiers standing over them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this accord with any observations that you had already made or were thereafter to make?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Well, having located the area of the graveyard in question, in answer to your question, having located the area, I did not observe them in the actual act of digging graves with HVO soldiers standing over them. This is what had been stated to me by Dutch transport battalion personnel. But I did see Muslim civilians standing around, about 10 or 15, with HVO soldiers with weapons nearby. To go on to answer your question, yes, I did see other instances of Muslim civilians, specifically an incident that took place on the southern approach to the Kaonik bridge. I can't give a precise date, but it will have been at that time, where I observed them digging trenches. There was a -- what was clear to me, a trench system, and they were digging them with armed HVO soldiers standing over them. And I can recall at least one elderly person there, an elderly man; possibly a woman as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And the arms that the HVO had, what type?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: These were Kalashnikov rifles, slung over their shoulder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please point out, on whichever map you find convenient, either the place where you saw people that related to the DutchBat complaint or the other incident to which you have referred?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: In relation to where I saw Muslims after having been told that they were being made to dig graves, it was actually adjacent to a graveyard to the northeast, the northeast area of Busovaca, around here [Indicates]. There were actually two or three graveyards, and I actually visited about three before I found the right one. The second incident, at the Kaonik [Realtime transcript read in error "Konjic"] bridge, it was to the south, actually in the area where I had witnessed the firefight I related to on the morning of the 25th of January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Major, although you were there for some time and know it live, if you call it "the Konjic [phoen] bridge," it comes out slightly strange on our LiveNote system; but if you can call it "Kaonik," then it will make the note easier for us to follow. Did you make subsequent attempts to get the sides together in Busovaca, that being work that was later taken over by Jeremy Fleming?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: That is correct. I would say that the last meeting I held between what I would call these local level commanders was on or around the 30th, perhaps the 31st of July, but when I saw the ceasefire agreement on the 30th, I knew that this had been formally taken over. What I was conscious of then was ensuring that I wasn't interfering with or causing some confusion, particularly to HVO and BiH representatives, as to who was leading this. So I felt that I'd finished the initiative that I had taken up from the 25th of January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 1st of February, did General Morillon chair a meeting at the Bila school and was an agreement signed by Blaskic, Hadzihasanovic and Morillon that all external forces should be withdrawn from Busovaca, there having been troops such as the Ludvig Pavlovic from Capiljina stationed in Vitez involved in clashes there and in Novi Travnik, and had there been references in this meeting to external HVO groups, such as the Alpha Force in Gornji Vakuf, the Black Shirts in Kiseljak, and on the Muslim side, Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, that is correct. I would state that I was not present at that meeting, nor would I have been. It was a high-level meeting chaired by General Morillon, and I was told that an agreement had been made and had been signed. But it was largely picking up from the agreement which had been signed on the 30th of January. As far as the formations which you mentioned there are concerned, I can recollect being told about them at the time, as indeed I would have read about this and other things in milinfo summaries and at the daily 5.00 conferences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Busovaca at the time occupied by a Kiseljak HVO battalion?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, having been briefed at the time, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, in the course of your duties, keep notes of various important events?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I kept two notebooks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you eventually been able to find those notebooks in your house or your temporary house in England?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: I found them, I think, about ten days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And extracts of those have, Your Honour, been provided to the Defence. If and when the witness refers to those notes, it may be helpful to the Chamber if he puts them on the ELMO in the way I think another witness did, without them necessarily becoming an exhibit, unless anybody wants them to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if you can shuffle the papers, as is appropriate. You don't necessarily need to take one document off; you can lay one on top of it quite conveniently. Did you on the 3rd of February find yourself tasked to go to Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was requested by the operations room, the operations officer, to go and see a man named Dario Kordic in relation to some things that he wanted to state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What had led to your going there? What had been the initial request?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: He had requested to see Colonel Stewart. He did not know me, and I, as I've already testified, was not aware of him. The nature of my duties -- in other words, I wasn't occupied at the time -- allowed me to go out as the senior representative in the battalion at the time. The commanding officer and the second in command were otherwise engaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following this first meeting, did you maintain regular contact with Kordic thereafter?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Yes. I then had a period between that day, the 3rd of February, and the 27th of February, and I saw Mr. Kordic for the last time. And whilst I have not recorded all the meetings, I would say I saw him approximately 15 to 20 times. Sometimes I saw him twice in one day, dependent on what might have been happening. So I would include those in the total.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your approach to Kordic, generally, and why?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Well, my approach to Dario Kordic was based on two things: Firstly, what I had experienced to date in my dealings with all commanders on all sides that I'd had to negotiate with; and secondly, on the first impressions which I gained from the first meeting on the 3rd of February. Would you like me to elaborate?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Relating to the first, that is the general impression I made. There was very little trust around on all sides. It was very difficult to get any form of negotiation going whatsoever. You had to work extremely hard at it, and you had to look for any angle that you could, to a degree exploit, to get people talking. You had to be -- you had to go out of your way to establish your credibility. The main thing was, if I said I was going to do something, I went to all lengths to try and get it done, so that I could establish some form of trust with the person who I was talking with; they would take me as a credible person, as a person of my word. So that was my approach to things in general with any, and I stress "any," person I was dealing with. With regard to Mr. Kordic, from the impressions of my first meeting, I saw that almost immediately -- I had been there in my fifth week of constant operations -- that he was one person who I could definitely do business with. It was clear to me that he exercised a lot of power, potentially a lot of power.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you respond to your assessment that he had power? How did you approach him?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Well, I decided that I needed to establish a good working relationship with him. And because I saw he was in a position of influence, power, then I actually treated him with a great deal of respect in the way that I addressed him, in my manner towards him. On the first meeting, certainly, and maybe on some subsequent meetings, I saluted him when I entered what was his working office in the basement of the PTT building in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this approach pay dividends?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: I would say that if I looked at the whole period, it paid dividends. It was a successful, professional relationship in terms of what I was able to achieve from the meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I wonder whether the witness could give us some of the indications that suggested to him that Mr. Kordic was a man of power.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think some of them will emerge later, but it would be helpful if the witness dealt with the first meeting and your first assessment. Before you come to that first assessment, I think it's fair to note that you actually made a nearly contemporaneous assessment of the man that is not included in either your statements or your summary, it is included in another document to which you've referred overnight; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: That is correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, indeed, I haven't got it written down, although you've told us about it. Tell us what the document is first that you've been able to refer to.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: It's a letter to my wife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sent when in relation to this first meeting?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: On the evening of the day that I had the first meeting with Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, now, with what may be contained there in mind, can you answer His Honour Judge Robinson's question about, first of all, early indicia of power, linking it, as you find it appropriate, to what you would discover later in general terms, recognising we are going to go through matters in detail?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just two things, Your Honour. We were provided last night with some extracts from Major Jennings' diary, for which of course we are grateful. We have not been provided with a copy of this letter, and in the absence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not surprising. You are not going to see his letter to his wife. If he's going to refer to any part of it, then of course it will be necessary to put it on the ELMO, something of that sort, but there is no need for the letter to be produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour, just the pertinent extracts, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that letter may still be in the hotel opposite, but it can be retrieved, or is it with you? Explain where it is.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: It is in my house back in England, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My mistake. And you refreshed your memory from it before coming here?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I return to the previous question, early indicia of power.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: This is in answering His Honour's question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: In answer to Your Honour, the -- relating to the impression which I made -- and I will try and be general, because there are instances of detail which I am going to go on to discuss. With regard to the first meeting, when I actually got down to what I would call a bunker, it was a reinforced with sandbags command centre. That was the immediate impression which I gained in the lower basement of the PTT building. Mr. Kordic sat at the head of the table, with uniform personnel down either side. There was a radio on the desk, and I believe a separate handset. And there was a room off to one side. I later discovered there was a fax machine in there, because that's where a fax came from that I was shown at the time. In terms of his manner, whilst being very correct and courteous, as he always was to me, as I was to him, in what he said and in how things were carried out with practically no discussion, I quickly formed the impression that he was clearly in charge. I was very interested, because he was a man that I felt that I could have negotiations with, dealings with, to get things done, an impression which I had not gained from any meetings that I'd had with other commanders, some I would describe as disappointing, almost shambolic in terms of the way conversation towed one way or the other. These are the meetings on the 27th, 28th, 29th of January with the lower-level commanders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the other uniformed -- the uniformed men in the room approach or react to Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: At this particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Very little was said by them, either in response to anything I had said -- I wouldn't say there was complete silence, but during the course of a meeting, which I believed certainly took place within an hour, probably about 40 minutes, the people who were doing all the talking were Mr. Kordic and myself. And they sat and listened very attentively. There was not much opinion offered. And this is in contrast to a number of meetings I'd had both with army BiH and HVO lower-level commanders, where sometimes it was -- I could describe a free-for-all, and arguments between various people at the table.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What communication systems appeared to be available to him?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Well, there were two handsets, and I'll be clear about what I mean by that, because you can have a handset which may be connected to a telephone or it may be connected to a radio. But I believe there was one of each: certainly a telephone in there, and also what I believed to be a radio. There was this fax machine which was next door, because I do recall on one occasion -- I haven't a date for it. I haven't a note for it in the notes which I made which have been presented to you, but I can recall a fax being brought through. I would say this was not in common in some headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you been informed in advance of any position apparently held by him?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Yes, I had. And I routinely went to the milinfo section before I went on any task to see if there was anything they could tell me about an individual I was going to meet or, indeed, an area that I was going to visit; what had happened in the last few days; who had said what; what, if anything, had been agreed. This was standard procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you knew what of his position or believed what of his position?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: I was told by the NCO, who was on duty in the milinfo section that morning, that he was known to be the vice-president of the HDZ; that he was young; an ex-journalist; that he had also been known to style himself or respond to the title "Colonel."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do by way of addressing him or deciding how to address him?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: When I went into the room, you had to go down two flights of stairs to get to the basement where what I would call his operations room was. As I entered the room, he was at the head of the table. It was a long room, with him -- a long table, with him at the far end of the room from the entrance you came in. So I assumed that it was him because of the layout of the room, but I wanted to confirm who I was talking to. And he stood up as I entered the room, so I got the feeling that it was him. So I addressed my question to him and I said, "Is it Colonel Kordic or Mr. Kordic?" And he said, "Da." He didn't answer the question. And I've been asked this many times, and that is my definite recollection. And it was -- I decided to call him Mister -- "Is Mister okay?" "Da." It was not referred to again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: On this occasion, as indeed on many other occasions, he, like everyone else, wore the dark, drab camouflage that I associated with HVO wearing trousers and would usually wear a dark t-shirt, not always, olive colour. He invariably wore what I would call a large crucifix, largish crucifix around his neck. No headdress.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anything said about whether he was in any sense a formation commander?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: If it had not been at that first meeting, it would certainly have been at a subsequent meeting that I would have tried to determine what his position was. And my recollection is I asked him, was he the HVO commander? And he said, "No." And I'm sure that I asked one or two more questions, but I never established from him by word of his own mouth what position he had, in terms of a title. He did refute that he was the HVO commander in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two other questions for short answers: whether, A, you met him alone; and B, just the detail of the protection before you ever got into the room.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: I was never alone in the room with him on any occasion. You had to get through two layers of protection. The first was the actual entrance to the PTT building, manned by armed HVO soldiers. You established who you were and you were told to wait inside at the top of the stairs. And then usually a wait of no more than one or two minutes and then you were led down the stairs and into the room that I described previously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Using the notes that you made, as you need, and laying them on the ELMO, if you do, can you tell us, please, quite swiftly, what was the nature of the complaints made at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Dario Kordic had, after we had exchanged courtesies, Dario Kordic -- and he also asked me who I was and what my position was and what I had in terms of numbers of Warriors. He then went on to make a number of complaints, which I listed in my notebook in his presence at the table. I think it would be easier if I laid these on the screen. Do you think it would be possible to get-- we may need to do them one at a time. I think it's easier, Your Honour, if I just relate to it, rather than making -- because these are notes I actually took at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, if you go through them fairly briefly, Major.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Just very briefly, the first one related -- basically he stated -- he was aware of the 30th of January ceasefire, and I actually had the document with me -- which is an exhibit, which we've already been through -- and he said, "Da, da, yes, yes, I'm aware of that. The BiH are the ones who have broken the ceasefire. I wish to make the following complaints." And they are serial numbered. The first related to three HVO soldiers who had been killed by army BiH, where they had been killed, where he believed the BiH soldiers had come from. In 2 -- can you move that, please -- a shelling that had taken place. So the first is actually a time, 15.45 hours on the 1st of February; the next one a shelling, that two civilians had been killed, Croat civilians, and a child. Another incident on the 3rd. This is probably the one which caused the most activity afterwards, because actions were taken as a result of these protests. And this, and over on the following page, relates to an incident or incidents in the area of the villages of Merdani and Katici, very close proximity to each other, which really purported to say that BiH dressed as HVO, with HVO emblems, had come and had taken up to 100 women, children, forcibly taken them away. They had lists of these people he could make available. And at this stage, the -- when I say "roadblock," because we're going to come on to discuss it, this is the blockage of the main Vitez/Zenica road, a significant blockage; about 100 metres of road was blocked as a result of an explosion. Efforts had been ongoing as part of the ceasefire agreements gauged first of all by Colonel Stewart and then General Morillon, the 1 February meeting; a precondition was the opening of that roadblock. He stated the HVO engineers had gone to look at it and they had been fired on by BiH. And as a result of these instances, he then said that he wasn't going to give any further assistance to removing the roadblock until their protection, the HVO engineers' protection, could be guaranteed, and that he was delaying the exchange of prisoners detailed in the ceasefire document by 48 hours. And these relate to notes I took at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: I then actually made a summary of the notes, and indeed a second summary. And this I actually made when I went back to the school prior to giving my information to the operations room and to the milinfo, which was a routine procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you set out there the taking of the women and children?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: He'd also talked about telephone communications --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just coming to that, yes?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go on, then.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: The telephone communications, this was a dispute that was probably going into its second week. The power had been supplied in some areas but not in others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, please, deal with item 4 of this report.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: We'll move up to -- and this is relating to the extensive roadblock which I just described. I realised -- we all realised this was a major stumbling block. It was going to take a significant effort to open this roadblock. It was a precondition to a ceasefire taking place. He said to me it was possible that assistance could be given to open this roadblock. And of all the things that were stated, whilst they were all very important, very important, this was the one that interested me in particular, as a company commander whose task was specifically to keep these roads open for the safe passage of humanitarian aid, as well as satisfying a major precondition which would have acted as a confidence-boosting measure to all sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was prisoner exchange delayed?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, the prisoner exchange was delayed for 48 hours, but an exchange of prisoners did take place subsequently. I was not involved in that -- the detail of that exchange of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turn to the last page of this part of the report. I think it continues on one further sheet.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Summarise the effect of that, please.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: There is a degree of repetition in this. It's a summary of a summary, actually. It all relates to the same 3rd of February meeting. You'll see in certain questions I've put a subsequent question; the question was for myself. In other words, I was taking the material and I was trying to work out what were the implied tasks; as a result of being given this information, what did I then have to go on and do? Because I wasn't just listening to protests and doing nothing about them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as a result of this first meeting, what assessments did you make? You told us about them in summary already, as supplemented by what you wrote to your wife and that you reminded yourself of before you came here.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Well, as I've already stated, and I will try and elaborate: As a result of having finished the meeting and pondered on what I'd been told, and also on my recollections of the meeting later that day, Dario Kordic was the first person that I had come across in five weeks of operations, dealing with a whole host of people, who gave me a good feeling that there was someone that I could deal with on a one-to-one basis, and if I could establish my credibility, I could get certain things done. I could, with his assistance, open the roadblock; open humanitarian aid; build up confidence between each side. And I saw it as part of my duty to cement that relationship. I have to say that the impression which I gained at that meeting, and in all subsequent meetings, was I did not like the person of Dario Kordic, in terms of how he conducted himself. He was a very loud person, a very arrogant person in approach -- and that is my personal opinion -- not somebody who I would have chosen to have dealings with subsequently, but I decided that I would, in order to get things done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your assessment of his military or civil powers and authority?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: At that stage, I was yet to see something happening on the ground. We had had a meeting and a conversation, if we are talking specifically about the 3rd of February.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: I was yet to -- to actually have concrete evidence of something that he had done that I could take or gain an opinion of, other than -- the impression I gained was that I went to see someone who had been described as the deputy president of the HDZ, and from my experience, five weeks' worth at that stage, I walked into what I took the impression of being a functioning operations room, with military personnel in there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a last question, if this is convenient to the Chamber, before what may be a break: What, if anything, of the fact that he said what he did about prisoner exchange, given the signatories to the ceasefire and so on?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Well, he stated to me --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Objection to this, Your Honour, and that is that there is no deadline for prisoner exchanges imposed in the document that has been marked as Exhibit Z421,1A, and I would certainly hope that the Trial Chamber has that in mind as this testimony is considered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you want this piece of evidence, Mr. Nice? If so, perhaps you could rephrase the question to make it plain what point you're making. The point, I understand, is that he wasn't a signatory to the ceasefire, and yet he was talking about prisoner exchange; is that the point?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, if any, significance did you find in his ability to talk about prisoner exchange, and why?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic stated to me that he was delaying the exchange of prisoners by 48 hours. What we were trying to establish, all of us, was who was actually in charge. This was not a straightforward thing. It wasn't up to that stage; it wasn't for the remainder of the tour I was there. And it was my belief, based on the chain of command I'd been told about, and the signatures to it, that that's what had been agreed, and suddenly this -- for the first time in my experience, certainly, there was a new name. There was a person there who had come into the equation, stating, "Well, I am delaying it by 48 hours."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn now for half an hour, so that will be 11.35. Mr. Nice, I notice there's a lot of material, but it would be helpful if you could get through the witness's evidence in chief by the luncheon adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I certainly hope to. There is a lot of material, and I'll just do my very best --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- and lead wherever I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you can deal with that. Of course, the material at the moment is dealing directly with one of the accused, but one hopes it can be dealt with as briefly as possible. Major, could you please be back in half an hour, and could you remember, in this and any other adjournments there are in your evidence, not to speak to anybody about it, and that does include the members of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major Jennings, bearing in mind we must move at a slightly brisker pace, if we can. Next paper exhibit in the stack, the two photographs, very quickly, if you can just take them. In the stack. Tell us what they show.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm sorry. This is not on. It doesn't need to be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is on, but -- yes.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: This relates to my activities subsequent to the 3rd of February, and I decided to make the opening of the roadblock on the Zenica road my main objective. I discussed this with Colonel Stewart. I had his approval. It was done properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This picture shows what?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: And this picture shows a lorry which had been drawn across the road about 500 metres from the road blockage itself, actually denying me access to get at the road to even look at the lorry. I am there in the top picture talking to a HVO representative -- I don't know his name -- with my interpreter and a member of the ECMM. The bottom one is the same place, but from a slightly different angle. It shows the countryside around. I had to negotiate to get even the lorry removed before I could then actually move on to have a look at the roadblock itself. In my discussions with the engineer commander, I said that I had had a meeting with Dario Kordic. I was trying to establish the roadblock itself, where it was, what I needed to do to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any success with the lorry?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Eventually, yes. It was typical of something that could take up to two or three hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 31, paragraph 30 being slightly out of order. Paragraph 31, again without looking at your summary, if you would be so good. On the 6th of February, did you have a meeting?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Yes. I requested a meeting with Dario Kordic. I had, by that stage, been able to look at the roadblock and actually work out a military plan for its removal, which was heavily dependent on engineer support, the use of engineer equipment. My problem was assuring the HVO engineers and Dario Kordic himself that I would give the necessary protection to his HVO engineers. And the reason for this was that part of the blockage was probably between two and four tilt mines which had been placed under a lorry at the scene, not dissimilar to the lorry that you just looked at. The BritBat policy was not to use British engineers to remove mines. Dario Kordic had agreed that his men would remove them, but only if I could guarantee protection. So I had specifically gone to see him because I was not clear in my own mind where the front lines were, where I actually had to put my outer cordon of men. And we got down to the nitty-gritty of where positions were. Mr. Kordic, not unlike any commander I had dealings with, was reticent about giving information away, of where front line positions were. And this I could understand. Everyone was very cagey about getting information of where their troops were. It was all a matter of trust. And it became apparent that the map I was looking at was not very good; it wasn't very detailed. It was then that Mr. Kordic offered me a map to assist in identifying the specific villages, ridges, contours, tracks, streams, what have you. He gave an instruction, and a man went to another room and very quickly returned with the map which we've already used this morning in evidence. It's the map that I have here by my side. And this is the map which I then subsequently used, not only in this roadblock clearance operation, but for other operations subsequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's Exhibit 2781 and, as the Chamber can see, it has JNA at the top of it. On that same 6th of February, did you hear anything of Muslims in the area of Katici?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: I cannot say that the passage which is related there, that is, immediately after the incident relating to the map, actually took place on the 6th of February or whether I was told about that on the 6th of February. What I can say is I did not observe such an incident taking place, that is, the use of the civilians as human shields. I was told about it at the headquarters in the course of my briefings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll deal then with a meeting, if there was one, where reference was made to what was happening in Gornji Vakuf. Explain briefly how such topics came to be discussed.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: This passage relates to a conversation that took place probably later, in February. I have not a date for it. And the reason it is there is that as part of trying to develop a relationship with Dario Kordic, I tried to end meetings by inviting him to talk about things of a more general nature; I mean, more generally in the area of operations; to try and talk in a more relaxed way. And the subject of Gornji Vakuf came up. And I merely stated and had noted with interest that he seemed to be aware that there were difficulties with ongoing negotiations to try and achieve a ceasefire in the Gornji Vakuf area. It seemed to me to be a long way outside of what I perceived to be his area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll return to paragraph 32 later. Paragraph 33, again, without looking at the document yourself, when did you start the removal of the roadblocks? There may be a date error that we've got to correct.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Well, I definitely started it on the 7th of February, the following day. It was a Sunday. And I started it as soon as possible after first light, because I envisaged it was going to be a long operation. And as soon as I had got my cordon in place -- what I mean by that is my soldiers in armoured vehicles in, as it were, a ring around the area we were going to do it -- I then commenced the operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you discover from the HVO engineer who was there something about the condition of the vehicle cab?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Yes. The things that -- the things had proceeded very well. The first thing we had to do was remove the tilt mines from underneath the lorry and then we had to actually drag the lorry away. After we had removed the tilt mines, the HVO engineer -- I would say commander, the person who had been shown to me to be in charge of the engineers in that particular party, that's the title I would give him, then talked about some form of assistance in moving an object or building or what have you, and was pointing to things on the ground. And I said, "Well, I don't know anything about this. We are moving a roadblock." And he then said, "Well, there is still an explosive in the bonnet."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: Well, I realised -- well, everyone left the area immediately, because we were right next to the lorry, and we obviously had to ensure the safety of all personnel, so all British, French -- because there were French U.N. there assisting us -- and the HVO engineers themselves, all left the area. We went about 100, 200 metres away. It was clear to me that something had gone wrong and I wasn't going to get any further with the HVO engineer representative there. So as it was Dario Kordic who I had gained the approval of to assist in removing the roadblock, I decided to go and see him straightaway. I have to say I was slightly concerned because I felt that if things went wrong and we stopped, we would not clear the roadblock. There had been so many occasions where it had come to a halt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Press on.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: I then went to see Dario Kordic in his headquarters and gave him a brief resume of where we had got to. He then started talking about putting an object in place. Actually, there was a very small T-junction next to the roadblock itself, and I wasn't clear what this was, and this is when he actually drew an object in a notebook which I was carrying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next two sheets of the notebook, please. Explain, please.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: The object at the bottom of the two pages -- this is a different notebook to the one you saw before -- was a hand drawing, you can see it there at the bottom in outline, a hand drawing of what turned out to be what I would call a prefabricated concrete object. I got the dimensions of it and the approximate tonnage, and what Dario Kordic was requesting was BritBat's assistance in moving this and putting it on the T-junction next to the roadblock. Now, at this stage I was in a very difficult position, because I had something in the region of over 200 French and British personnel on the ground, in position, the promise of getting a roadblock opened which had been blocking the road for nearly two weeks, and the prospect of things coming to a grinding halt. And I therefore took the decision on my own initiative to say -- and the words I used, "I will see what I can do about it." As a result of that, he then said, "Okay, we can press on." I then returned to the position, and when I returned, the HVO clearly had received some message to the effect that the unblocking of the road operation could continue. I omitted to say that in saying I would see what I could do, I said I couldn't do anything that day; I would look at it the following day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you in fact have any intention of giving the help he required?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS
utterances.text: When I looked at that, there was no way I could give any assistance with regard to what would have been, in effect, establishing the infrastructure of a checkpoint -- as I would have to neither side, to maintain impartiality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
